what: what is seen through the bridge windows, and the display of light over the round well
prompt:
Edit this photograph, picture 1. Change only what is seen through the bridge windows, and the display of light over the round well. Everything else stays exactly as it is, in the same place and at the same size: Jugger, the face, the hands, the clothes, the room and every light that falls on them.

THE WINDOWS. Through every window is the sea this ship sails, at its true size, exactly as the reference pictures show it: black space sown with fine white dust, and far off the wall of a vast hollow sphere, a net of thin dim blue lines in six-sided panes. Close by, drifting past the ship, stands a coral of bricks of light, flat-sided rectangular blocks with deep indigo and violet faces and thin bright edges, set edge to edge in rings round open holes with a spray of white needles in every hole. It is one thing seen through all the windows, running on behind the frames from one pane to the next. Two long ribbons of small amber gold bricks curve away past it, the trails of small craft flying guard, and a swarm of tiny violet shards streams toward the ship. The window frames stay where they are. The glass is thick and scratched and carries faint reflections of the bridge.

THE DISPLAY. The old display is gone, and all of its light with it. Over the well stands one closed dome of light, like a model under a glass bell: its round foot sits inside the brass rail, its top is lower than the window sills, and no part of it reaches a window, a console or Jugger. Everything it shows is inside it, and nothing glows outside its edge. It is a hologram with real depth: a small solid-looking scene with a near side and a far side. Inside it, small, is the same sea as in the windows: one great dark ship, no longer than a forearm in the display, shaped like a closed scallop shell: a low swept fan of ribbed plates spreading back from a domed bridge at its point, with a row of round engine mouths glowing along its wide stern edge and thin bright seams between its plates. Swarms of tiny violet shards are closing on it from every side, each swarm flowing like a shoal, and where they have fed, plates are gone from the fan and the frame shows. Three tiny bright craft circle the ship, and each lays behind it a long curving ribbon of small glowing amber gold blocks set end to end, flat-sided, with deep clear faces and thin bright edges, the three ribbons winding round the ship like a cage. A coral of indigo blocks set edge to edge in rings round open holes drifts beside it, pale lilac crystals shaped like twelve-sided dice hang in the dark, and far behind curves the wall of a vast hollow sphere, a net of thin dim blue lines in six-sided panes, in black space sown with fine white dust. The raised gauntlet is held just above the dome, over the place on the ship where plates are gone.

REFERENCE PICTURES, in the order they are given. Pictures 2 to 4 are the real sea Jugger sails: in picture 2, a small bright craft, cyan plates on a dark frame, flying at a coral of indigo bricks of light, each brick a flat-sided block with a deep blue face and thin bright edges, set in rings round open holes with a spray of white needles in each; two wide bands of amber gold light run over the coral; behind them, black space sown with white dust and the far net of six-sided panes; in picture 3, a coral of orange bricks edged in red, set in rings round open holes, holding a pale lilac crystal with many flat faces; rows of small blue dashes curve through the dark, and a swarm of tiny violet shards flows in the shape of a ring; in picture 4, the heart of the sphere: a glowing lime-green ball, long thin indigo beams and red rods standing through the dark, orange and violet corals, and clouds of tiny orange and violet shards. Whatever of that sea this picture holds, beyond a window or small in a display, has exactly that look: the same shapes, the same colours, the same glow. Take the look and never the framing. No reference is copied whole, and no craft in them is Jugger's. Picture 5 is the great ship itself, the same ship from four sides: a low dark ship like a closed scallop shell, a swept fan of ribbed plates spreading back from a domed bridge at its point, a row of round engine mouths glowing orange along its wide stern edge, thin bright seams between the plates and one small cyan crystal behind the bridge. Wherever this picture shows that ship, small in a display or from outside, it is this ship.

It stays one photograph taken with a real camera: the new parts have the grain, the focus and the exposure of the rest and meet it without a seam. Nothing in the picture carries writing, numbers or a symbol.
